record.title: ProbeGuard reports risk-controlled abstention from medical answer-consensus trajectories
record.summary: Wang et al. introduce ProbeGuard, which uses the formation history of a multi-round medical question-answering consensus to decide when to abstain. Its process features track agreement, minority persistence and retrieval; for immediately unanimous answers it also checks rationale agreement and probes with counter-evidence. On MedQA, the authors report a process-score AUROC of 0.696 versus 0.512 for terminal agreement. Their stratified Learn-then-Test rule answered 55.3% of the unanimous layer at 9.0% observed risk against a 15% target across 50 splits, under an assumption that calibration and deployment questions are i.i.d. within each stratum. In specialty analysis, emergency medicine had 19.1% realized risk at the same layer-level threshold, and was not separately certified. These are author-reported multiple-choice benchmark results, not clinical deployment evidence.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On the authors’ MedQA multi-round RAG substrate, ProbeGuard’s process score achieved 0.696 AUROC for distinguishing correct from incorrect consensus, versus 0.512 for terminal agreement. The authors evaluated three 8B backbones and several medical QA benchmark sets.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: For the immediately unanimous MedQA layer, the paper reports 0.553 coverage at 9.0% observed selective risk against a target α=0.15 across 50 calibration/test splits. The distribution-free risk statement assumes calibration and deployment questions are i.i.d. within each fixed stratum.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Under the layer-level threshold, the emergency-medicine subgroup had 19.1% realized risk at target α=0.15; this specialty-level breakdown was descriptive and was not separately certified.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The counter-evidence probe had median latency of 114 seconds and 4,381 completion tokens per probed MedQA question, compared with 72 seconds for the underlying answer process; it is applied to the unanimous subset.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper evaluates multiple-choice medical QA with one published consensus substrate and three 8B backbones; it does not establish prospective clinician-use, free-text clinical performance, or safety in deployment.

evidence_gaps.description: Independent reproduction of the discrimination, calibration, subgroup and cost results.
Prospective performance and calibration under real clinical case mix, free-text workflows and clinician routing.
Availability of the paper-linked code and data could not be confirmed in this activation.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported process-sensitive abstention results transfer to clinical decision-support systems, detecting correlated consensus errors while controlling answered-case risk could materially affect how medical agents are evaluated and deployed. The score reflects that conditional consequence; the evidence is a single author-run multiple-choice benchmark and does not show clinical effectiveness.
limitations: Results are reported by the paper authors; no independent reproduction was performed.
The 15% selective-risk bound assumes calibration and deployment samples are i.i.d. within each fixed stratum.
Emergency medicine had 19.1% realized risk under the aggregate layer threshold; the subgroup was not separately certified.
Evaluation uses multiple-choice medical QA, one multi-round retrieval substrate and three 8B backbones; no clinician-use or prospective deployment was studied.
The active probe adds a median 114 seconds and 4,381 completion tokens per probed MedQA question, versus 72 seconds for the underlying answer process.
brief.summary: Wang et al. introduce ProbeGuard, which uses the formation history of a multi-round medical question-answering consensus to decide when to abstain. Its process features track agreement, minority persistence and retrieval; for immediately unanimous answers it also checks rationale agreement and probes with counter-evidence. On MedQA, the authors report a process-score AUROC of 0.696 versus 0.512 for terminal agreement. Their stratified Learn-then-Test rule answered 55.3% of the unanimous layer at 9.0% observed risk against a 15% target across 50 splits, under an assumption that calibration and deployment questions are i.i.d. within each stratum. technical.claimed_result: On MedQA, authors report 0.696 AUROC for the process score versus 0.512 for terminal agreement. The calibrated rule answers 0.553 of the unanimous layer at 9.0% observed risk for target α=0.15 over 50 splits. Emergency medicine has 19.1% realized risk under the layer-level threshold, without separate specialty certification.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint specifies a benchmark protocol and reports author-run results on MedQA, MMLU-Pro medicine, MedMCQA and a hard-frontier reference, using Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and HuatuoGPT-o1-8B. No independent reproduction or clinical workflow study was performed.
technical.mechanism: ProbeGuard derives abstention signals from an agentic RAG system’s execution log: agreement trajectory, persistent minority answers and retrieval saturation. For a first-round unanimous answer, it adds mutual-entailment scoring over rationale conclusions and an active retrieval probe for counter-evidence. A stratified Learn-then-Test procedure selects answer thresholds from calibration data.
technical.regime: Multiple-choice medical QA with a published multi-round RAG substrate, three 8B backbones and benchmark datasets. The risk guarantee assumes calibration and deployment examples are i.i.d. within each fixed stratum. Specialty analysis is descriptive under the aggregate layer threshold.
technical.reproducibility: No code execution or independent reproduction was performed. The paper-linked GitHub URL was reported inaccessible in a prior read-only check; no conclusion about deletion follows.
technical.strongest_baseline: For MedQA process discrimination, terminal agreement achieves 0.512 AUROC, near chance; first-round agreement reaches 0.677. The paper compares several abstention signals on the same substrate but does not provide an external clinical baseline.

brief.title: ProbeGuard reports risk-controlled abstention from medical answer-consensus trajectories
brief.why_it_matters: A unanimous panel can share the same misconception, so final agreement alone may hide error. The paper tests whether interaction traces and targeted counter-evidence can support abstention decisions with a stated statistical bound. Its aggregate guarantee depends on within-stratum distribution stability, while the emergency-medicine subgroup and probe cost show why deployment would need case-mix monitoring, specialty-level calibration and workflow evaluation.
